evals.prompt: We're running DevForge, a 130-person weekend hackathon in Rotterdam. Demo day wraps tomorrow at 5pm with all teams presenting in the main hall. I still have the attendee survey from our annual API conference (overall satisfaction 1-10, session ratings, venue and catering ratings, likelihood to return, one open comment box) - can you adapt it for the hackathon and tell me when to email it out? We had 14 volunteer mentors floating between tables, a 5-judge panel picking winners, and three sponsors provided the APIs teams built on. The main thing I personally want to know is whether teams will keep building their projects after this weekend.
evals.expected_output: A hackathon-specific instrument (not a reworded conference survey) with team dynamics, mentor, judging, tooling and continuation dimensions; the main survey captured in-room at demo day; continuation measured by a separate short follow-up 1-2 weeks later; anonymity on for judge and mentor ratings.
expectations: The response states that the conference survey alone is insufficient for a hackathon and adds hackathon-specific dimensions rather than only rewording the conference questions.
The instrument includes a team formation or team dynamics question (for example ease of forming teams, collaboration quality, or willingness to work with the same teammates again).
The instrument includes a question on mentor availability or mentor usefulness.
The instrument includes a question on judging fairness, clarity of criteria, or transparency of the decision.
The instrument includes a question on the quality of the sponsor-provided APIs, SDKs, documentation, or tooling.
Project continuation is measured with a separate short follow-up survey sent one to two weeks after the event, not solely by a question on the demo-day instrument.
The follow-up is described as a second, distinct instrument rather than a delayed or re-sent first survey.
The response explains that asking about continuation on demo day itself only collects intention, not behaviour.
The main survey is collected in-room at demo day (a form, code, or prompt at closing), using the captive moment while the day can still be planned, rather than defaulting to the requested email send.

Anonymity is turned on for the instrument or at least for the judge and mentor rating questions, with the reasoning that respondents who suspect the rated person will read their name give unusable ratings.
In-room collection is justified with a materially higher response-rate band than email (roughly 40-60% versus 10-30%, or described as a multiple of the email rate).
The in-room capture moment is tied to a line in the day's run of show or explicit coordination with whoever runs the day.
The response does not propose emailing the main survey days later as the primary collection channel.

evals.prompt: Post-mortem question on our survey. CloudCamp Lyon ended nine days ago. We sent our feedback survey by email six days after the closing keynote - one send, 23 questions - to all 480 attendees. 22 responses so far. Honestly I think this proves our attendees just don't care enough about the event to bother answering. Should we accept that and plan next year assuming low engagement?
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis that the collection failed (late send, long instrument, single send), not that attendees are indifferent; a salvage plan (one reminder, shortened instrument, possibly an incentive) and a corrected design for next edition, with the response rate stated beside any finding.
expectations: The response computes or states the response rate (roughly 4-5%) and compares it against the published emailed band of roughly 10-30%, or a floor of roughly one in ten.
The response explicitly rejects the conclusion that attendees do not care: a below-floor rate means the collection failed, not that the audience is indifferent.
The six-day delay is identified as a cause, naming a 24-48 hour send window as the standard.
The 24-48 hour window is presented as practitioner consensus rather than a measured effect, and no percentage improvement is quoted for send timing.
The 23-question length is identified as a cause, citing that a very short survey more than doubles the median response rate of a long one, stated as a ratio rather than invented point precision.
The response recommends sending a reminder now, capped at no more than two reminders in total.
The response warns that additional reminders beyond that cap produce fatigue rather than more responses.
The response recommends shortening the instrument toward a short core of roughly 3-5 questions.
The response recommends cutting every question that has no named decision behind it, rather than trimming by topic or taste.

An incentive or prize draw is presented as a legitimately available lever in this specific situation (prior rate below the band floor and the event already over), with event-specific prizes preferred over generic gadgets.
The response notes that in-room capture is no longer available for this edition and records it as the plan for the next one.
The user is instructed to state the response rate beside any finding drawn from the 22 responses rather than presenting the answers as a verdict.
The response does not claim the 22 responses are representative of the 480 attendees.

evals.prompt: For HackTheHarbor, our 90-person student hackathon ending Sunday, here is my feedback plan: a fully anonymous survey so people are honest, questions asking hackers to rate each of our 6 judges by name on fairness, a rating of their assigned mentor, plus general satisfaction. To boost responses, everyone who completes it gets entered into a draw for an iPad. We'll also publish the best quotes in our recap blog post. Can you sanity-check the plan and write the intro text for the survey?
evals.expected_output: The anonymity-versus-prize-draw contradiction is surfaced and resolved before fielding (keep anonymity, drop the draw); the anonymous/confidential promise is named in the intro text; publication consent is added at collection time or the recap quotes are dropped; free-text handling is planned.
expectations: The response flags the contradiction that an anonymous survey cannot run a prize draw, because the draw needs an identifier attached to responses.
The response requires choosing one before fielding, and does not paper over the conflict with a workaround such as anonymizing after the draw.
The recommendation is to keep anonymity and drop the draw, because the instrument rates judges and mentors by name.
The anonymity rationale is stated as mechanical, not merely ethical: a respondent who suspects the judge or mentor will read their name gives a rating that cannot be used.
The response distinguishes anonymous from confidential as two different promises and says which one is being made.
The chosen promise is stated inside the survey intro text the response drafts.
If any incentive is retained in the plan, an event-specific prize is recommended over a generic gadget like an iPad.
The response flags that publishing quotes requires publication consent asked at collection time, because an anonymous respondent cannot be asked afterwards.
A publication-consent question or checkbox is added to the instrument, or the recap-quote plan is explicitly dropped.
The response plans who reads raw free-text responses, on the grounds that free text will name people.
Any quote destined for publication is redacted of names.
The response notes that a code-of-conduct-type allegation arriving in free text is routed to the code-of-conduct process immediately rather than treated as a survey finding.

evals.prompt: Here's my draft survey for ShipItCon, our single-track conference (220 attendees, happened yesterday): 1) Did you enjoy our amazing speaker lineup? 2) Rate your overall satisfaction 1-10. 3) Rate the content 1-10. 4) Rate the venue 1-10. 5) Rate the catering 1-10. 6) Would you attend a paid workshop day next year? 7) How was the venue? 8) How did you hear about us? 9) What is your job title? 10) Which social networks do you use? ...and 21 more in the same style, ending with 32) Any other comments? I figured more questions means more insight. Can you polish the wording so it flows better?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to merely polish: the survey is rebuilt decision-first and cut to a short core of 3-5 questions, leading and hypothetical questions replaced with behavioural ones, the open box bounded, and the send treated as urgent given the event ended yesterday.
expectations: The response does not simply polish the wording of all 32 questions; it restructures the survey around cutting.
Each question is tested against the decision it would change, and questions with no named decision behind them are cut.
The length trade is stated to the user: a very short survey more than doubles the median response rate of a long one.
The final instrument lands at roughly 3-5 questions.

The question 'Did you enjoy our amazing speaker lineup?' is flagged as leading or unfalsifiable and replaced with a behavioural question such as which sessions the respondent attended or left before the end.

The question 'Would you attend a paid workshop day next year?' is flagged as hypothetical and replaced with a past-behaviour question, such as whether the respondent has paid for a workshop day at another event in the last two years.
The unbounded 'Any other comments?' box is replaced with a bounded question such as the one thing to change for next edition.
The four separate 1-10 rating scales are collapsed rather than all kept, on the grounds that multiple stacked scales get answered on autopilot as one blended impression.
The question 'How was the venue?' is either cut or rewritten to surface concrete obstacles rather than collect a polite 'fine'.
The closed-versus-open balance is respected: mostly closed-ended questions, with open-ended questions capped at three to four.
Because the event ended yesterday, sending within the 24-48 hour window is stated as urgent.
The send plan includes one reminder days later and at most two reminders total.
Demographic or curiosity questions such as job title and social networks are cut unless tied to a named decision, and no new questions are added from a generic question bank.

evals.prompt: Survey results are in for KernelDays: 300 attendees emailed, 74 responded, survey was anonymous and we never asked any consent question. Two free-text answers worry me. One says 'Marta Keller's talk was a train wreck, she clearly hadn't rehearsed and blew past her slot by 15 minutes.' Another describes a sponsor's booth staffer repeatedly cornering and touching attendees at the afterparty. My plan: forward the first one verbatim to Marta so she can improve, email the second one to the sponsor's account manager so they deal with their staffer, and quote the funniest positive comments verbatim in our public recap. Good?
evals.expected_output: All three planned moves are stopped: the speaker complaint goes through the owned per-speaker pass-through rather than raw and direct; the afterparty account is a code-of-conduct report routed immediately to that pipeline, not to the sponsor; verbatim quotes stay unpublished because consent was never collected from anonymous respondents. Findings are themed with counts and the response rate stated.
expectations: The response rejects forwarding the speaker complaint verbatim and directly to the speaker.
The response states that what a speaker receives, and its timing and framing, is owned by the speaker-experience side of the operation rather than decided ad hoc from the survey.
The afterparty account is identified as a code-of-conduct allegation, not a survey finding.
The allegation is routed immediately to the code-of-conduct reporting pipeline.
The response rejects sending the allegation to the sponsor's account manager as the handling path.
The allegation is handled now, not queued to the end of the survey analysis.
The response refuses to publish verbatim quotes, because publication consent was not asked at collection time and anonymous respondents cannot be asked afterwards.
Any theme or paraphrase that is shared is redacted of names.
Free text is grouped into themes with counts rather than forwarded raw.
The response rate (74 of 300, roughly 25%) is stated beside the findings.
Raw response exports are not handed to anyone downstream; a summary is handed over instead.
The material that eventually reaches the speaker is her per-speaker summary (ratings and comments minus abuse) through the owned pass-through, not the raw insult.

evals.prompt: Board update time for DataStack Summit, second edition, 850 attendees. Survey numbers: overall satisfaction 4.1/5, 58% say they are likely or very likely to return, operations rating 3.6/5, 210 responses from the 700 attendees we emailed. Sponsors: 6 surveyed, 2 answered, and one of the two ticked 'will not sponsor again'. I want to roll all of this into one event score out of 10 for the board slide - something like 8.2/10 - and file the sponsor stuff into the appendix. Can you compute the blended score and draft the slide?
evals.expected_output: The blended score is refused; the slide presents one number per metric with response rates per role, the 58% return intent is flagged as below the early-warning threshold, and the sponsor who will not renew triggers an immediate call rather than an appendix row.
expectations: The response refuses to compute the single blended score, explaining that satisfaction, return intent, and operations answer different questions and averaging them produces a number nobody can explain.
The slide presents one number per metric: satisfaction, return intent, and operations reported separately.
The 58% return intent is flagged as below the roughly two-thirds early-warning threshold.
The return-intent trend is marked for hand-off to the cross-edition improvement process rather than resolved inside this edition's findings.
The sponsor who ticked 'will not sponsor again' triggers an immediate phone call, not an appendix row to analyze later.
Sponsor verdicts are passed onward to whoever manages sponsor relationships immediately rather than at the end of the analysis.
The 2-of-6 sponsor sample is treated by name, not by percentage: no sponsor-satisfaction or sponsor-response percentage is presented as meaningful.
Response rates are stated per role (attendees separately from sponsors), never as one blended number.
The attendee response rate (210 of 700, 30%) is stated beside the attendee findings on the slide.
Free-text results appear as themes with counts, not as an unquantified mood summary.
The findings are framed as input to the team's own debrief, and the response issues no go/no-go verdict on the event itself.
The summary includes what the instrument failed to ask, inferred from what open answers kept raising unprompted.

evals.prompt: PlatformCon Oslo is in three weeks - 350 developers, single day on a Thursday, ending with a closing keynote and prize ceremony at 5pm. For feedback I was going to do what we always do: email the survey the Monday after, and offer a $75 Amazon voucher raffle to push responses up. Last year that combo got us about a 19% response rate. Two volunteers are free on the day if that helps. Anything you'd change?
evals.expected_output: The channel moves to in-room capture at the closing keynote (day still plannable, captive moment, day-of capacity available), with a run-of-show line added; the voucher raffle is demoted because its promotion condition is not met; the email backup goes out within 24-48 hours instead of Monday, with at most two reminders.
expectations: The response promotes in-room capture (a code or form at the closing keynote) as the primary channel instead of the planned email.

The promotion is justified by the conditions that make it available: the day is still being planned, a captive closing moment exists, and day-of capacity (the two volunteers, or one more line in the day plan) is available.
The response requires adding a line to the run of show, or coordinating with whoever runs the day, for the capture moment.
The channel move is justified with the response-rate multiple: in-room lands roughly 40-60% against roughly 10-30% for email.
The response does not cite 85-95% as an in-room response rate; if that figure appears it is labelled a completion rate (the share who finish once started), a different quantity.
Channels are compared on response rate only.
The voucher raffle is demoted: with last year's 19% inside the emailed band rather than at or below its floor, and the day still open, the condition that would promote an incentive is not met.
The response notes the incentive is the costliest option on effort and on compliance exposure (prize administration, and an identifier attached to responses) while buying less than the channel move.
The response notes that a raffle requires identifying respondents, which conflicts with any anonymity promise the instrument might need.
If any prize is kept, an event-specific prize is recommended over the generic voucher.
The Monday send is corrected: the email follow-up for people missed in-room goes out within 24-48 hours of the Thursday close, not the following Monday.
The email cadence includes at most two reminders.
The response distinguishes owning the survey's question set from owning the email's copy and cadence, rather than treating them as one deliverable.

evals.prompt: ByteWorks Conf wrapped on Friday - 240 attendees, 7 invited speakers. Should the speaker survey just be the attendee survey with extra questions bolted on? My plan was to add 10 speaker-specific questions to the end of the attendee form and send everyone the same link. I also want to report 'speaker satisfaction: 71%' if 5 of the 7 respond, and compare it against last year's 83%.
evals.expected_output: Speakers get their own instrument measuring organizer performance, not a longer shared form; at 7 speakers a personal note may collect more than a form; speaker results are treated by name, not as a percentage; the year-over-year comparison is handed to the cross-edition process.
expectations: The response rejects one shared form with speaker questions bolted onto the attendee survey; speakers get their own module or instrument.
The speaker questions measure organizer performance - pre-event communication and information supply, venue and presentation equipment - not the quality of the speaker's own session.
The speaker instrument includes whether the speaker achieved what they came to do, or how engaged the audience was.
The speaker instrument includes whether they would recommend qualified peers as future speakers.
The response raises that with only 7 speakers, a short personal follow-up message can collect more than a form does.
The 'speaker satisfaction: 71%' statistic is refused: a population of 7 is treated by name, not by percentage.
The comparison against last year's 83% is handed to the cross-edition trends process rather than performed as part of this edition's findings.
What each speaker receives from attendee ratings, and when, is routed through the speaker-experience side rather than sent directly from the survey analysis.
The attendee survey stays short rather than growing to accommodate the merged speaker questions.
The send is treated as urgent given the event ended Friday, invoking the 24-48 hour window rather than scheduling it later in the week.
Attendee and speaker response rates are reported separately, never blended into one number.

evals.prompt: GreenGrid Conf just finished its fourth edition - we run it yearly and already publish a recap post every year. 205 of the 610 attendees answered the survey. Results are mixed: talks rated well, but the venue wifi and the lunch queues got hammered in the open comments - 41 comments on wifi, 28 on lunch. My co-organizer says we should quietly keep the survey internal so sponsors don't see the negatives; I think we should at least email respondents a thank-you. What do we actually do with these results, and who decides?
evals.expected_output: Respondents get a you-said-we-changed note as the floor; a public findings post is promoted because the event compounds and a recap is already planned, including the negatives; publication sign-off sits with the team's debrief; themes carry counts with the response rate beside them.
expectations: The response rejects keeping everything internal with nothing back to respondents, naming the compounding cost: respondents who hear nothing do not answer next year.
The recommended floor is a you-said-we-changed note: a thank-you plus 2-3 findings being acted on and what will change.
The note is preferred over a bare thank-you because a respondent seeing their own answer move something is what builds next edition's response rate.
A public findings post is promoted in this specific case, because the event compounds across editions and a recap is already planned.

The published version includes the negative findings, with publishing what went wrong (ideally including what the survey design itself got wrong) framed as the established precedent rather than a risk.
Wifi and lunch appear as themes with their counts (41 and 28).
The response rate (205 of 610, roughly 34%) is stated beside the findings.
Publication consent collected at survey time is checked before any verbatim comment is quoted; without it, quotes stay out or are reduced to redacted substance.
Publication sign-off is owned by the team's debrief process; this workstream supplies the survey half.
The whole findings summary goes to the debrief before the debrief meeting, not during or after it.
Talk ratings and the wifi/lunch operational complaints are not averaged into one overall score.
The note back to respondents includes the headline number and confirms the answers were read.
